chapter_theme: In the Renunciation sarukkam a sage tells the king which kinds of people are low and how rare is a human birth, shows pleasure as honey over a pit, names the four paths of effort and spends the rest on giving: its three grades, the giver's seven qualities, its fruit in kingship and the harm of giving to the cruel.

1978.reading: Asked who the Koodar, Milechchar and Kumanudar are, the teacher answers: those who, spinning endless quibbles, weigh good qualities and yet will not accept them, and have nothing good in them.
1978.nuance: The verse opens a list of lesser kinds of men and names them only by their quibbling; the three labels are the teacher's, and the outsider word மிலைச்சர் is used here as a term of low standing, not as a tribe the verse describes.

claims.claim: those who quibble endlessly over virtues and refuse to accept them are base and not truly human

1979.reading: The same low company includes those of unrestrained lineage who cannot be restrained, those who eat flesh together with other forbidden things, and those who begin deeds that the high-minded never begin.
1979.nuance: The verse measures the low by what they eat and do, not by birth alone, though line 1 speaks of lineage. Line 2 is hard: the word விடங்கார் may be 'poison-black' or a damaged form, so exactly what is eaten is not fixed.

claims.claim: eating flesh and starting deeds that the noble avoid mark a low kind of human

1980.reading: Among such births some become these kinds, some sink into low states and dwindle away soon after joining, and others, the teacher says, are past the reach of knowledge.
1980.nuance: The verse lists fates after the types of 1978-1979 without naming them, and its last half-line is hard to construe, so it is read loosely.

claims.claim: some low births pass quickly into lower states and are beyond ordinary knowing

1981.reading: Even among those born in the lands where humans live, within the two and a half continents, many are no better than hangers-on, for their efforts never join the three classes.
1981.nuance: The 'two and a half continents' is the Jain measure of the human world; the three classes are not named here, and the comparison to kinsfolk (ஒக்கல்) may rather mean 'like the household's hangers-on'. Both are uncertain.

claims.claim: birth in a human land does not make one fit for the three classes of people

1982.reading: Those mingled with the three classes who are fools in a crowd and cannot judge what is fit and unfit are not to be called people, and the king is told to treat them as chaff thrown aside.
1982.nuance: Humanity is made a matter of discernment (தக்க தகா), not of birth; this is the teacher's judgment, spoken to a king who must himself discern.

claims.claim: one who cannot tell the fit from the unfit is not a true human being

1983.reading: Good lands and good forms are not found just where one chooses to be born, so to pass beyond the countless wombs and reach them is very hard.
1983.nuance: The verse says good births are hard to win; it does not say here by what means, which 1985 gives.

claims.claim: good birth in a good land is very rare among endless wombs

1984.reading: No one counts the eunuch, the blind and the like as human, and even when everything else is in order, birth as a woman is not an honoured one.
1984.nuance: This is the teacher's view in a Jain work, set among marks of a lesser birth, and the epic gives it without reply here; it is the epic's view of women's standing as a birth, not a general truth about women. The first word அண்ணை is obscure.

claims.claim: birth as a woman is not an honoured birth
the eunuch and the blind are not counted among humans

1985.reading: Of the eighty-four hundred thousand kinds of birth, only those who hold firmly to a gladdening good deed come to this human body.
1985.nuance: The figure 84 lakh of yonis is the classical Jain count of kinds of birth; the verse makes karma the sole means of reaching the human body.

claims.claim: the human body is won only by those firmly holding good karma, out of 8.4 million kinds of birth

1986.reading: Even a child who, from the first days in the womb, forms and grows without fault will meet many sufferings that cannot be fully told.
1986.nuance: The verse puts the pain of life before birth, so even a fair birth is not a good fortune.

claims.claim: suffering begins in the womb and cannot be avoided even by a faultless birth

1987.reading: The infant crosses the harsh wilderness of childhood and the faults of youth; if one gets through the forest with difficulty, one reaches old age and, failing, goes to another state.
1987.nuance: Life is drawn as a wilderness with three stages; the 'other state' (கதி) is the next birth, not extinction.

claims.claim: life, with its stages from infancy to old age, ends in passage to another state

1988.reading: As a man chased by an elephant hangs over a deep pit with a snake in it and licks a falling drop of honey, so the king should weigh the pleasure of human life.
1988.nuance: This is the well-known parable of the man hanging in a pit between an elephant and a snake; the verse gives its parts compactly and does not say what gnaws the rope, so the image is read in its common form. It makes pleasure real but small, not unreal.

claims.claim: human pleasure is only a drop of honey tasted while death and birth threaten on every side

1989.reading: For two people living together in love, wanting pleasure, many sufferings arise with the ties between them; the verse is read as saying that without these ties effort would be wholly work.
1989.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are hard: the sense of முற்றும் தொழிலே is not fixed, and the verse may say that without those ties effort would be pure labour.

claims.claim: household love and desire bring many sufferings with their ties

1990.reading: For those born into this state there is one lasting thing, won by vows: the firm effort that leads to the golden lands of the heavens and of enjoyment.
1990.nuance: The reward is the heavens and enjoyment lands, not release; the epic does not here say vows lead to liberation.

claims.claim: vows lead to the heavens and lands of enjoyment

1991.reading: Though the ways of firm effort are many in telling, count them as four: one's own conduct, giving, austerity and worship.
1991.nuance: The first of the four, தன்னியல், is read as one's own conduct; the verse gives no more than the list, and 1992 onwards deal with the second, giving.

claims.claim: the many ways of effort fall into four: conduct, giving, austerity and worship

1992.reading: Giving is said to be of best, middle and lowest grade, depending on a faultless receiver, the giver and the gift, and the gift itself must be beyond reproach.
1992.nuance: The three grades are named, but which factor ranks a gift first is not said here. Compare the seven qualities of the giver in 1995.

claims.claim: the worth of a gift depends on the receiver, the giver and the gift

1993.reading: The verse tells of givers who have mastered the senses and think of future births rather than this life, and whose faultless merit comes back to them multiplied threefold.
1993.nuance: The first lines use rare words (ஐமை, இமைபதம்) and cannot be fixed; the threefold multiple is clear from line 3 but what the three are is not.

claims.claim: a gift made with thought for later births returns merit multiplied

1994.reading: Wise people list renunciation, restraint, doing good to others, guarding kin and holding to truth as duties, and the teacher has given giving as the quality of one who lacks nothing and fits the receiver.
1994.nuance: Both halves are hard to join and the last line may speak of the receiver rather than the giver.

claims.claim: renunciation, restraint, kindness to others and care of kin are named as duties, with giving one among them

1995.reading: The giver's seven qualities are listed: patience, capacity, eagerness to give, love for the receiver, non-attachment, discernment and the absence of regret.
1995.nuance: Only the count of seven is plain; several words of lines 1-2 (போதிசை, பொன்றுதறு, கட்பம்) are rare, so the names are read from the context and not fixed.

claims.claim: a giver must have seven qualities, among them non-attachment and absence of regret

1996.reading: One who is himself restrained, gives to the restrained and feels the hurt of all living things, grows in knowledge and conduct and reaches the blameless lands of joy.
1996.nuance: The syntax of the second line is hard, so the verse is read with some doubt.

claims.claim: a restrained giver who feels the hurt of all lives gains knowledge and conduct and reaches lands of joy

1997.reading: Those who, seeing the distress of the people at the door, give food as far as they can will become kings with armies, elephants and umbrellas.
1997.nuance: The fruit is kingship in a later birth; this ties the giving to the king's own rank, which Payapati ties to past deeds in 1843.

claims.claim: giving food to the hungry bears fruit in a later birth as a king

1998.reading: One who gives to evil-doers wealth that causes many injuries and harms to lives will earn a fruit the teacher would only laugh to tell.
1998.nuance: The mock tone of 'I would laugh to say it' is the teacher's. This makes harmlessness (கொல்லாமை) a limit on giving.

claims.claim: giving harmful things to those who do evil is no gift and brings a bad fruit

1999.reading: He is like a man who loses his own wealth and builds for himself the door to a wretched state, or hands great wealth to cruel wretches and asks them to serve him.
1999.nuance: The simile finishes 1998: the one who gives to cruel men gets his own harm back.

claims.claim: giving to cruel men is self-destruction, not a gift

2000.reading: The gifts made to those fit to receive by one who has grasped the true principles do not fall among the three grades, but lead him up among the best of the gods.
2000.nuance: The 'three grades' may be those of 1992 or the fruits of the gift in three realms; the verse is hard and its reading uncertain.

claims.claim: gifts of one who knows the true principles lead among the best gods

links.note: 1982 refuses the name 'people' to those without discernment; 1984 adds the eunuch, the blind and woman's birth to those not counted as fully human.
links.teaches: The speaker's two tests of being human are discernment and the kind of birth, and the second does not follow from the first.

links.note: 1989 shows household love bringing sufferings with its ties; 1990 offers vows as the one lasting course for those born in this state.
links.teaches: The sage sets vows as the answer to the pain that household desire cannot remove, which 1989 only states.

links.note: 1998 refuses merit to giving harmful things to evil-doers; 1999 compares such a giver to one who feeds the cruel and asks their service.
links.teaches: The comparison turns a moral rule about giving into a plain foolishness, so a listener sees harm to the giver and not only a fault.

links.note: 1992 grades gifts into best, middle and lowest by receiver, giver and gift; 2000 says gifts of one who knows the principles are not placed within three grades.
links.teaches: The gift of the knowing giver is said to go beyond the three-grade scheme, so the grading does not describe the highest case.

links.note: 1843 has Payapati say that his umbrellas and bowing kings are a gift of his good-deed deity; 1997 says the givers of food become kings with armies and umbrellas.
links.teaches: The earlier remark that kingship is earned acquires a stated source: a gift of food to the hungry becomes the umbrella.

links.note: 1992 grades a gift by the receiver's fault-lessness, the giver and the gift; Tirumanthiram 508 sends giver and receiver to hell if the receiver does not bow in worship of the Lord.
links.teaches: The two ask what makes a receiver worthy and give different answers, so one cannot tell from either how to judge a fit receiver.

gains.a: The Jain scheme lacks a test of worship: it names no receiver whom a gift would harm the giver by reaching.
gains.b: The Saiva verse lacks a grading of gifts and a role for the giver's own qualities, which it reduces to the receiver's bowing.

links.note: 1992 treats giving as graded with a lowest grade; Tirumanthiram 505 says gifts to those without conduct and vows are like milking a barren cow.
links.teaches: The lowest grade of giving may still be a gift, and the Tirumanthiram says that at some point there is no crop.

gains.a: The grading gains a limit below which a gift is wasted, which 1992 does not name.
gains.b: The barren-cow image gains a scale: the poem shows that giving is not simply worth or not worth, but graded.

links.note: 2000 says the gifts of one who knows the true principles lead him among the best gods; Tirumanthiram 1867 says charity to tireless ascetics sinks deep karma and becomes the golden world.
links.teaches: One text places the fruit of giving in a higher birth, and the other in the removal of karma, which are different ends.

gains.a: The Jain verse gains a different reward, since removal of karma is not what it names, only a birth among gods.
gains.b: The Saiva verse gains a condition: here the giver's knowledge of the principles is part of the reward, not only the receiver's austerity.

links.note: 1988 pictures pleasure as honey tasted by a man hanging above a pit with an elephant and a snake; Naladiyar 60 says the higher ones see the pain in any pleasure and do not cling.
links.teaches: The parable explains why fools do not renounce: the honey is real, and the danger is out of sight while one tastes it.

gains.a: The parable gains a statement of what the wise do while the honey drops, which the image does not give.
gains.b: The quatrain gains an image for the fool's blindness, so that his not renouncing is shown as enjoyment of a real sweetness.

links.note: 1985 says only those who hold firmly to good karma come to the human body, out of eighty-four lakh births; Naladiyar 34 says to take the great fruit of the rare body.
links.teaches: The epic gives the count and cause of the rare body that the quatrain only calls rare, so the urgency has a reason.

gains.a: The count of births gains a use: the rare body is to be pressed for fruit like cane.
gains.b: The 'rare body' gains a measure and a cause: eighty-four lakh births and firm good karma.

links.note: 1987 draws childhood, youth and old age as a wilderness ending in another state; Naladiyar 11 says the wise renounced in childhood, knowing grey hair would come.
links.teaches: The epic shows what lies past old age, another birth, and so the quatrain's renunciation at the start is not a mere fear of aging.

gains.a: The wilderness of life gains an answer: renounce early, before the other state.
gains.b: Old age gains a sequel in another birth, which the quatrain's staff and grey hair do not name.

links.note: 1997 promises the giver of food a later kingship; Kural 222 says that even if there were no higher world, giving alone is good.
links.teaches: The epic's giving is promised its fruit, and the Kural says it is worth doing without one, so the reward is a bonus to a duty and not its ground.

gains.a: The promise of kingship gains a test: would the giving stand if there were no later birth.
gains.b: The Kural's 'even if no higher world' gains a case of the world's usual motive, the later kingship.

cast.role: the teaching sage who instructs the king on the rarity of human birth and on giving; unnamed in these verses and taken to be the sage the ministers sought in chapter 80
King Payapati, addressed as the garlanded one and the king (கோவே, மன்ன)

source_issues: The teacher is not named in 1978-2000; he is taken as the sage Payapati's ministers proposed seeking in chapter 80, from the sarukkam, and the addressee as the king (1997 கோவே, 2000 மன்ன).
1979 line 2, 1981 line 4, 1993 lines 1-2, 1994, 1995 lines 1-2 and 2000 turn on rare or damaged words; their readings are marked uncertain or hedged in nuance.
